scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that social groups shape identity, then argues individual choices matter just as much; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Each of us belongs to many groups, from our family and nation to our friends, faith, and profession.
Some people argue that it is primarily through our identification with social groups that we define ourselves.
I agree that groups play a powerful role in shaping who we are, but I do not believe they define us more than our own choices and experiences do.
First, the groups we belong to clearly shape a great deal of our sense of identity.
From birth, our language, values, and habits are largely learned from the family and culture around us.
For example, people often describe themselves first by their nationality, religion, or profession when asked who they are.
This shows that group membership gives us a ready-made sense of belonging and a shared story to live by.
Belonging to a group can also give people pride, support, and a clear set of expectations to follow.
Much of what we believe and value would look very different had we been raised among other people.
To this extent, social groups are a genuine and powerful source of identity.
Second, however, we are defined just as deeply by our own choices, talents, and inner lives.
People raised in the very same family or culture often grow into strikingly different individuals.
Consider two siblings who share a background completely yet hold opposite beliefs, careers, and dreams.
Such differences show that identity is shaped from within as much as it is handed down from outside.
We also define ourselves by the groups we reject, the values we question, and the paths we deliberately choose.
A person who leaves the religion or country of her birth is still very much defining who she is.
Our individual decisions, then, are at least as important as the groups we happen to join.
In conclusion, social groups do play a large part in shaping our identity.
But our own choices, experiences, and inner character matter just as much, if not more.
In truth, we are best understood not as products of our groups alone, but as individuals who shape ourselves within and against them.
